# Getting started

## Install Java

Ichthyop is a Java program. Therefore, Java is required.

-   Download the most recent version of Java here: <https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/>

-   Install Java

-   Open a `Terminal` or a `Cmd` prompt and type:

```
java -version
```

::: callout-warning
**Java \> 11 is required!**
:::

## Install NetCDF {.smaller}

Ichthyop also need the NetCDF-C library to run.

**Linux**

Open a Terminal and type:

```
sudo apt install netcdf4
```

**Mac Os X**

Open a Terminal and type:

```
sudo port install netcdf4
```

**Windows**

Download the pre-built libraries in [Unidata website](https://docs.unidata.ucar.edu/netcdf-c/current/winbin.html)

::: callout-warning
During the install process, make sure that the location of the library is added to the `PATH`
:::

## Download Ichthyop

-   Create a `ichthyop` folder
-   Go to <https://github.com/ichthyop/ichthyop/releases/latest>
-   Download the `ichthyop-X.Y.Z-jar-with-dependencies.jar` binary file, replacing `X.Y.Z` by the actual Ichthyop version number.
-   Move the `.jar` file in the `ichthyop` folder

## Download hydrographic files

-   Download the hydrographic sample files on the Ichthyop Zenodo Community: <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10890689>
-   Move the `.zip` file in the `ichthyop` folder
-   Unzip the archive file

## Running Ichthyop

**Windows**

-   Double-click on the `ichthyop-X.Y.Z-jar-with-dependencies.jar` file.

**Linux/Mac Os X**

-   On the Terminal, navigate to the location of the `ichthyop-X.Y.Z-jar-with-dependencies.jar` file using `cd`
-   Type `java -jar ichthyop-X.Y.Z-jar-with-dependencies.jar &`

# First simulation

## Creation new configuration

-   Create a new configuration file by clicking on the `New` button (@fig-new)

![New configuration](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ichthyop/ichthyop/master/doc/console/_static/step1-configure.png){#fig-new fig-align="center" height="200px"}

## Choosing template

-   Select the `Generic` template
- Remame your configuration file (for example, `first_ichthyop_run`
- Click on `Create` (@fig-template)

![Choosing template](img/generic-conf.png){#fig-template fig-align="center" height="600px"}

## Running the simulation

-   Preview the simulation by clicking on the `Preview button` (@fig-prev)

![Preview simulation](img/preview.png){#fig-prev fig-align="center" height="300px"}

-   Run the simulation by clicking on the `Run simulation` button (@fig-run)

![Running simulation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ichthyop/ichthyop/master/doc/console/_static/step2-simulate.png){#fig-run fig-align="center" height="200px"}

## Visualization

-   Visualise the results by clicking on the `Make maps` button (@fig-map)

![Mapping outputs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ichthyop/ichthyop/master/doc/console/_static/step3-mapping.png){#fig-map fig-align="center" height="450"}

## Expected results

You should see larval dispersal off Cape Town in South Africa (@fig-conf1).

![Outputs of the first simulation (advection)](img/conf1.png){#fig-conf1 fig-align="center" height="500"}

# New simulations

::: callout-note
In order to keep track of your different experiments, we advise you to create a dedicated configuration file with a consistent name (for example `roms-noadvection.xml`, `roms-advection-growth.xml`, etc.)
:::

## Exploring configuration file

-   Explore the different processes and parameters contained in the configuration file and their default values (@fig-edit)

![Exploring configuration file](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ichthyop/ichthyop/master/doc/console/_static/edit.png){#fig-edit fig-align="center" height="500"}

## Deactivating advection

-   In the configuration file, go to:

```{mermaid}
   flowchart LR
   id2(Transport)
   id3(Advection)
   id2 --> id3
```

-   Disable advection by clicking on the `Enabled` tick box
-   Save the configuration file by clicking the `Save` button.

::: callout-warning
**Remember to save the configuration file after every change**
:::

-   Run the simulation
-   Draw map
-   **What happens?**

## Playing with advection/diffusion

Activate horizontal diffusion in a similar way:

```{mermaid}
   flowchart LR
   id2(Transport)
   id3(Horizontal dispersion)
   id2 --> id3
```

-   Make experiments with diffusion only, with both advection/diffusion and compare the results.

::: {#fig-adv-diff-exsp layout-ncol="4"}
![No advection/No diffusion](img/conf2.png){#fig-noadv_nodif}

![Diffusion only](img/conf3.png){#fig-noadv_dif}

![Advection/Diffusion](img/conf4.png){#fig-adv_dif}

![Advection only](img/conf1.png){#fig-adv-nodif}

Results of the different Ichthyop configurations
:::

## Displaying particle depths

-   In the `Mapping` section, choose to represent the `depth` variable, with values -50, -30 and -10 m for minimum, medium and maximum, respectively.
-   Click on `Make maps`
-   What do you see?

## Vertical migration

-   In the configuration file, go to:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
id1(Biology)
id2(Movements)
id3(Vertical migration)
id2 --> id3
id1 --> id2
```

-   Read the explanations at the top of the block. Click on `Enabled` and look at the default values of the parameters.

-   Run the simulation with larval vertical migration and display the results. Is there anything wrong?

- Go to the

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
id1(Simulation)
id2(Output)
id1 --> id2
```

and correct the record frequency to save outputs every three hours. Remember that, as indicated in the console:

$$
N_{freq} = \dfrac{F_{out}}{\Delta t}
$$

with $N_{freq}$ the record frequency parameter, $F_{out}$ the output frequency (**in seconds**) and $\Delta t$ the simulation time-steps (**in seconds**), which is available in the `Simulation - Time` section.

What value should we put for the record frequency to have outputs every 3h?

- Set the new value for the record frequency parameter and re-run the simulation. Visualize the results.

- What do you see now?

- Have a look at the `Note that the depth of larvae is now changing according to the vertical scheme specified, but that this movement has almost no effect on the overall larval distribution (@fig-mig2).


::: {#fig-migration layout-ncol="3"}
![](img/vert2.png){#fig-mig1 width="100px"}

![](img/vert3.png){#fig-mig2 width="100px"}

![](img/vert4.png){#fig-mig3 width="100px"}

Different migration configurations. (a) No migration (b) Migration between -10 and -30 m (c) Constant depth (-50 m)
:::

## Growth

-  Deactivate vertical migration and reset tthe record frequency to 144.

-   Go to:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
id1(Biology)
id2(Growth)
id3(Linear Growth)
id1 --> id2
id2 --> id3
```

-   Read the explanations at the top of the block and activate growth
-   Run the simulation and visualise the `length` variable using `Auto range`
-   Now change the dispay and visualise the `stage` variable using `Auto range` for the values and colours.
-   How do you interpret the results?

# Release methods

## Initial positions in a text file

Unselect vertical migration and growth. Go to

```{mermaid}
    graph LR;
    id2(Release)
    id3(Drifters from text file)
    id2 --> id3
```

Enable the block.

Click on the `New` button inside the `Value` field. Name your file `benguela_drifters.txt` and click on `Save`.

A window will pop-up. Read the explanation at the beginning of the file. Run a simulation.

Display the particle trajectories by putting `depth` as the display variable.

![Trajectories simulated in Ichthyop and plotted in R](img/drifter-release.png){#fig-drift width="300px"}

## Release zones

In Ichthyop, disable

```{mermaid}
    graph LR;
    id2(Release)
    id3(Drifters from text file)
    id2 --> id3
```

and enable:

```{mermaid}
    graph LR;
    id2(Release)
    id3(From zones)
    id2 --> id3
```

On the `Zone file` section, click on `New`. Rename the zone file `benguela_zones.xml` and click on the `Save` button. Have a look at the Zone editor interface.

The actual zone file contains one release zone (`Release`) and one destination zone (`Recruitment`). These zones are defined by the geographic coordinates of a polygon, two isobaths (`Bathymetric mask`) and upper and lower depth (`Thickness`).

Preview the simulation to verify that the zone is properly set (@fig-preview-release).

![Preview of release zone](img/preview-release.png){#fig-preview-release width="300px"}

What do you have only one zone displayed?

Run the simulation and visualise larval depth.

Duplicate the previous release zone by setting different release isobaths:

-   500m - 1000m
-   1000m - 2000m

You should now have three differents release zones. Preview the release zones (@fig-preview-mulrel). **Make sure that all release zones have the same `Thickness` settings**

![Preview of multiple release zones](img/preview-multiple-release.png){#fig-preview-mulrel width="300px"}

Run the simulation. Look at the trajectory as a function of release zone (@fig-traj-mulrel).

![Distribution of larvae as a function of the release zone](img/multiple-release-traj.png){#fig-traj-mulrel width="300px"}

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
## Destination zones
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
## Destination zones (1)
:::

Go to:

```{mermaid}
    graph LR;
    id1(Biology)
    id2(Recruitment)
    id3(In zones)
    id1 --> id2
    id2 --> id3
```

Look at the parameters defining recruitment and at the recruitment zone. What is the distinction between a release zone and a recruitment zone?

Click on the `Edit` button in the `Zone file` parameter section. Select the previously defined zone file.

Check with `Preview` that the 3 release zones and the destination zone appear (@fig-rel-rec)

![Preview of the three release zones and of the recruitment zone](img/preview-rel-rec.png){#fig-rel-rec width="230px"}

Run the simulation and look at the trajectories

In Main - Time, add two new release dates for days 8 and 13 (same year, month and hour) by clicking on `Add value`. In Main - Output, change the directory in which the simulation results are stored to `output\TP1`. Save, run the simulation, this time there are 3 simulations, one for each release date.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
## Destination zones (2)
:::

Open the compute_recruitment_Ichthyop_v3_TP function in the R software. Adjust the path to the TP1 directory, install the XML package if necessary, then execute the function (@fig-recr1).

Go back to Ichthyop and visualise the trajectories of individuals for the first release date (@fig-recr2). Note that in the end there is no individual inside the destination area! Look again at the parameters used for recruitment to understand why the percentage of individuals transported from the release zones to the destination zone, as computed with the R function, is not zero.

::: {#fig-reczone layout-ncol="2"}
![](img/recr1.png){#fig-recr1 width="230px"}

![](img/recr2.png){#fig-recr2 width="120px"}

Mean (and standard error of the mean) transport success from 3 release zones to a destination zone, for 3 release dates. The zones are shown in (b) with the final distribution of individuals for the first release date.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
## Destination zones (3)
:::

Add now 2 new destination zones defined by isobaths 200–300 m and 300–500 m respectively. To avoid that individuals recruit in several zones, change `Stop moving when recruited` to True. In Main - Output, change the directory in which the simulation results are stored to `output\TP2`. Save, run the simulation.

Open the compute_connectivity_Ichthyop_v3_TP function in the R software. Adjust the path to the TP2 directory, install the fields and spam packages if necessary, then execute the function (@fig-recr3). Go back to Ichthyop and visualise the trajectories of individuals for the first release date (@fig-recr4). Note that the final positions of individuals in the north are very different in @fig-recr2 and (@fig-recr4). Why?

::: {#fig-reczone-bis layout-ncol="2"}
![](img/recr3.png){#fig-recr3 width="230px"}

![](img/recr4.png){#fig-recr4 width="120px"}

Mean transport success (a) from 3 release zones to 3 destination zones, for 3 release dates. The zones are shown in (b) with the final distribution of individuals for the first release date.
:::

## Dispersal distances

In TP2, delete the folder containing the simulation maps of the previous simulation, leaving only the 3 .nc files (that correspond to the 3 release dates). In the R software, open the compute_distances_Ichthyop_v3_TP function and adjust the path to the TP2 directory. Install the sp package if necessary and then execute the function (@fig-disdis). Do the same for TP1 (change the values of xlim and ylim in the hist function of R if necessary).

![Histograms of dispersal distances for the 3 files (corresponding here to 3 release dates).](img/disdis.png){#fig-disdis width="300px"}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
## Backtracking (1)
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
## Backtracking
:::

From the final positions of the simulated drifters trajectories (`Initial positions in a text file` section above), we're going to backtrack (i.e., track backwards in time) each drifter to its initial location.

In Main - Advanced - Release, choose the `restart mode`. Read the explanation of the block and choose the NetCDF file that corresponds to the output of the drifters simulation performed before. If you forgot which file it is, or deleted it, then do it again!

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
## Backtracking (2)
:::

In Main - Time, click on `Show hidden parameters` and for `Direction of the simulation` select `backward` instead of `forward`. Now we need to adjust the time for `Beginning of the simulation` to make it correspond to the end of the simulation performed forward in time, i.e. `year 01 month 05 day 18`.

Save, run the simulation and then plot the trajectories using the same script as before. Note that the trajectories are perfectly back-simulated (compare @fig-back with @fig-drift) except for a few of them which are missing (because the individuals were `dead` at the end of the simulation forward in time, for reaching the border of the domain).

![Trajectories backtracked in Ichthyop and plotted in R](img/back.png){#fig-back width="230px"}
